# Brahma Saṁyutta (SN 6)
**ID:** SN 6
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Brahmasamyutta* (SN 6) is the sixth chapter of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, situated within the verse collection (*Sagāthāvagga*) [Bodhi 2003; Norman 1983]. Translated as "Connected Discourses with Brahmās" or "Linked Discourses With Divinities", the section comprises fifteen discourses centering on high celestial beings of the Brahma realm, most prominently Mahābrahmā and Brahmā Sahampati [Bodhi 2003; SuttaCentral]. In early Buddhist texts, these deities are portrayed respectfully as beings reborn in exalted realms through meritorious kamma who frequently act as champions of the Buddhist dispensation, while remaining subject to delusion and future rebirth [SuttaCentral]. Key narrative episodes include Brahmā Sahampati's entreaty to the newly awakened Buddha to teach the Dhamma (SN 6.1) [Bodhi 2003; SuttaCentral], as well as visits by the Buddha and disciples—such as Mahāmoggallāna, Mahākassapa, Mahākappina, and Anuruddha—to cure the pride of Brahmā deities harbouring wrong views of their own permanence or supremacy (e.g., SN 6.4 with Baka Brahmā and SN 6.5) [Bodhi 2003; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. The samyutta also includes the *Kokālikasutta* (SN 6.10), treating the fate of Kokālika and listing ten cold hells [Yifa and Romaskiewicz], and concludes with the *Parinibbānasutta* (SN 6.15), commemorating the Buddha's passing [Norman 1983; SuttaCentral].
Many discourses in the collection share substantial material with other canonical and non-Pali works. SN 6.4 shares its prose opening with the *Brahma-nimantanika Sutta* (MN 49) and corresponds to the *Baka-brahma Jātaka* (Ja 405) [Bodhi 2003]. SN 6.15 includes Brahmā's eulogy at the Buddha's decease as found in the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* (DN 16), though it reverses the order of verses spoken by Ānanda and Anuruddha and omits the attainment of cessation (*saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti*) [Norman 1983; Walshe 1987]. All fifteen suttas have parallels across Chinese Āgama collections, primarily preserved in the *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99) and the "Alternative" *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 100), with several discourses matched in the *Ekottarikāgama* (T 125) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus confirms substantial text reuse with these Chinese collections, and aligns SN 6 verses with Sanskrit and Tibetan works, including the *Mahāvastu-avadāna* (which preserves parallel traditions to SN 6.1) [Bodhi 2003; DharmaNexus], the *Saṅghabhedavastu*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra*, the *Patna Dharmapada*, and the *Āyuḥparyantasūtra* [DharmaNexus], alongside related verse parallels in the *Lalitavistara* and *Catuṣpariṣatsūtra* [Levman 2014].
